value: wild-caught feral frogs were attracted to chemical stimuli from a newt (Taricha granulosa) held in a mesh pouch rather than deterred, in short 10-minute choice tests
units: categorical (time in aquarium zone next to newt pouch, centre, or away)

source.authors: David Anderson, Olivia Cervantez, Gary M. Bucciarelli, Max R. Lambert, Megan R. Friesen
source.title: Feral frogs, native newts, and chemical cues: identifying threats from and management opportunities for invasive African Clawed Frogs in Washington state

method: behavioural: two-choice aquarium test, mesh pouch with a newt versus an empty mesh pouch (sham control), time in zones scored over 10 min, linear mixed-effects model with Tukey post hoc tests
conditions: Feral X. laevis captured from stormwater ponds in Lacey and Issaquah, Washington, and housed in a captive facility (holding time not stated); each animal randomly selected from the husbandry facility. 50 choice tests in a 38 L aquarium with 2 L aged tap water, 25 with the newt pouch on the southwest side and 25 on the northeast side to rule out side cues; the other pouch was empty. The number of individual frogs and whether any were reused is not stated. Newts were wild-collected rough-skinned newts held at least two weeks and agitated for one minute before trials. Zones: next to the newt, Centre (middle fifth) and Away (the empty-pouch section and the section adjacent to it). Results pieces: Tukey post hoc tests found all pairwise comparisons significant; Newt vs Away p = 0.003; mean time Away 210.6 s (+/- 4.9 s SE) and next to the newt 368.5 s (+/- 5.1 s SE) (zone areas unequal; means not used as the value). The same paper's tadpole experiment (Rana aurora tadpoles) is a separate result and is not part of this value. Stimulus is a live newt in a pouch; no concentration of chemical measured.
quote: However, our short-duration experiments found that X. laevis were attracted to newt chemical stimuli rather than deterred.

value: free-ranging white storks approached unmown fields sprayed from an ultralight aircraft with a green leaf volatile mix ((Z)-3-hexenal, (Z)-3-hexenol, hexenyl acetate, the smell of freshly cut grass)
units: categorical (stork approaches to sprayed fields; chi-square)

source.authors: Martin Wikelski, Michael Quetting, Yachang Cheng, Wolfgang Fiedler, Andrea Flack, Anna Gagliardo, Reyes Salas, Nora Zannoni, Jonathan Williams
source.title: Smell of green leaf volatiles attracts white storks to freshly cut meadows

method: field experiment: aircraft-sprayed green leaf volatile mix on unmown fields, with plane-only and water-spray controls, stork approaches observed from the air and the ground
conditions: Free-ranging wild storks of one village population (roughly 70 individuals, Boehringen, Germany), some carrying GPS tags; no animal handled in the experiment. Four independent spray trials (monitored area 5 x 6 km, 49 storks present on 27 Apr 2018 and 37 on 2 Jul 2018) drew 9 independently approaching individuals or groups from 0.5 to 1.2 km away (pieces of the Results); only the combined total is reported, not per trial. Controls: the ultralight plane alone, or water sprayed from it, did not elicit any reactions in storks residing at the same or shorter distances (Results piece); chi-square comparison with the volatile spray, chi2 = 11.7, N = 15, df = 2, p = 0.003 (tool summary). Storks outside the 45 degree downwind band did not approach (n = 7) and storks upwind of a field never approached (tool summary). A separate single trial with a truckload of cut grass drew 3 approaching individuals or groups, which left after about 10 min when no food was found. Spray dose and concentration at the stork were not measured. Order: observation of natural mowing, then the grass trial, then the spray trials.
quote: Furthermore, uncut fields that were sprayed with a green leaf volatile organic compound mix ((Z)-3-hexenal, (Z)-3-hexenol, hexenyl acetate), the smell of freshly cut grass, immediately attracted storks.
note: Whole abstract sentence of 29 words, read in three abutting pieces (ends verified). Authors, volume 11, issue 1, article number 12912 from Crossref single lookup; Crossref CC BY 4.0 (vor and tdm); the Nature page prints the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence. Ciconia ciconia has no sense_chemical record on main; DOI and s41598-021-92073-7 absent from the whole docs/ tree and from desk branches d22x to d25x. The reaction is a long-distance approach to a sprayed compound mix, not a detection threshold.

value: in forced-choice flight-tunnel trials with a UV-reflective film window beside a control-film window, 3 of 15 collision events were with the UV-reflective window and 12 of 15 with the control window
units: count of collision events (Wilcoxon matched-pairs test)

source.authors: John P. Swaddle, Lauren C. Emerson, Robin G. Thady, Timothy J. Boycott
source.title: Ultraviolet-reflective film applied to windows reduces the likelihood of collisions for two species of songbird

method: behavioural: flight-tunnel forced-choice trials, window with BirdShades UV-reflective film versus window with a control film, collision outcome scored from video, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test
conditions: Brown-headed cowbirds caught in a baited walk-in trap at a local farm and housed in an outdoor flight aviary (about one week in captivity before trials, tool summary); 18 cowbirds flown, 17 pairs analysed (Methods pieces: 'zebra finches N = 24, and brown-headed cowbirds N = 18'). Results piece: in 88.2% (N = 15 of 17) of the forced-choice 'both' trials cowbirds were judged likely to collide with either window; the quoted sentence gives the split of those 15 events (Wilcoxon, Z = 2.02, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.043). Control film had similar physical and spectral properties except for UV reflectance (tool summary; the authors call it a positive control; no untreated window). Each bird met each treatment on a separate day in balanced order (tool summary). In the control-versus-treatment comparison cowbirds were at least 30% less likely to collide with the treated window (Z = 3.29, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.001); the abstract's 75 to 90% (forced choice) and 30 to 50% (same film on all windows) ranges pool zebra finches and cowbirds. Cowbird flight speed near treated windows was a non-significant trend (p = 0.091). The second species, zebra finch, came from a 19-year stock colony and is not part of this value. Tunnel lighting simulated daytime; film UV reflectance was the manipulated variable, no UV spectrum of the windows is given here.
quote: Of these collision events, 20% (3 of 15) were with the BirdShades-treated window and 80% (12 of 15) were with the control-treated window (Wilcoxon, Z = 2.02, N = 17 pairs, p = 0.043; Fig. 6).

value: two of five commercial electric shark deterrents (E-Shark Force and NoShark) did not statistically reduce the likelihood of the bait or board being touched or taken by free-ranging sharks (null)
units: categorical (bait or board touched or taken; Poisson exact tests)

source.authors: A. R. G. Gauthier, E. Chateauminois, M. G. Hoarau, J. Gadenne, E. Hoarau, S. Jaquemet, S. K. Whitmarsh, C. Huveneers
source.title: Variable response to electric shark deterrents in bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas

method: behavioural: baited field trials at a harbour, a sardine on a 30 cm rope below a board carrying an active commercial electric deterrent or an inactive control, five-trial series in random order, GLMs and Poisson exact tests
conditions: Free-ranging bull sharks at Nouville harbour, New Caledonia, a former feeding site (feeding banned in 2017), 18 days in September 2019, 29 individual sharks identified (47% of passes identifiable); each series had one trial per deterrent and one control in random order, up to 15 min each. Trials per class (Results piece): Control 75, E-Shark Force 74, NoShark 78. Results pieces: the E-Shark Force and NoShark p values were p = 1.00 and p = 0.18; sharks interacted with bait or board 97.3% of the time at the control board (Results piece; the second Results piece 'ranging from 57.7% (Freedom + Surf) to 97.3% (E-Shark Force)' is not reconciled with it, so no percentages are used as the value). Contrary results in the same study: Freedom + Surf was the most effective deterrent, cutting bait takes by 42.3% (abstract piece), and Rpela v2 and Freedom + Surf Shortboard also lowered bait takes; bull sharks reacted significantly more near E-Shark Force and NoShark and had more passes before taking the bait than at the control board (Discussion pieces). No deterrent stopped bait takes completely, and effectiveness fell over time for the Freedom + Surf, Rpela v2 and NoShark (Results piece). The preceding Discussion fragment mentions an in situ measured intensity of 0.38 V/m (device not identified in the piece read); the study reports field measurements and modelling. The result concerns commercial products, not a detection threshold.
quote: Neither the E-Shark Force nor the NoShark statistically reduced the likelihood of the bait/board being touched/taken.

value: firefly larvae significantly selected snail mucous trails over distilled water or a no-trail control in two-plate choice tests
units: categorical (first plate occupied; exact binomial tests)

source.title: Prey-tracking behavior and prey preferences in a tree-climbing firefly

method: behavioural: two-plate alternative-choice test, mucous trail laid by a snail on a wood plate versus a plate with distilled water or no trail, choice defined as the first plate occupied by the entire body, exact binomial tests
conditions: Larvae and land snails collected on Ishigaki Island, Okinawa, in mid-October 2017 and kept under laboratory conditions at 24 C with a 13:11 light/dark photoperiod (Methods pieces; the paper does not say explicitly that larvae were wild-caught, the collection site implies it). Larval body size 30.2 +/- 8.0 mm and 0.20 +/- 0.21 g (n = 45); instar not stated; 15 replicates per comparison, 45 larvae in all (whether larvae were reused is not stated); trail side assigned randomly and trails used within 2 h (tool summary). Results pieces: mucus trail chosen in 13 of 15 replicates against no trail and 13 of 15 against distilled water, P = 0.0074 (tool summary reports the same figures for both comparisons); null: no-trail versus distilled water 11 of 15, P = 0.1185, larvae tended to choose distilled water more often than the no-trail plate. Staying-time paired t-test for mucus versus distilled water P = 0.0049 (tool summary). The snail species supplying the trail and the cue (chemical or tactile) are not separated by the design; the other experiments (prey species preference, predation trials) are not part of this value.
quote: P. atripennis larvae significantly selected mucous trails over distilled water or control (no-trail) treatments.
